candidateRows: Modern Western liberal, humanist, and secular values ultimately derive from Christianity and remain saturated with Christian assumptions.
This directly advances the Christian-inheritance side of the motion by identifying Christianity as the ultimate source of the West's prevailing values.
In his opening answer, Holland recounts how studying the alien moral world of Greece and Rome led him to trace his own liberal and humanist commitments back to Christianity.
The crucifixion radically reversed Roman valuations of power by giving dignity to victims, slaves, and people previously regarded as insignificant.
The argument offers a specific Christian mechanism for the emergence of human dignity, making it a direct causal case for the motion.
Holland contrasts crucifixion's Roman function as public degradation with Christianity's inversion of the symbol into triumph, dignity, and the elevation of the lowest.
Christianity largely repackaged older Near Eastern myths, while the conceptual framework of European culture was principally forged by classical civilization.
This supplies the principal alternative genealogy demanded by the motion, locating Western culture and ethical universality in pre-Christian sources.
Holland's claim that Christianity introduced a radical moral transformation centered on the crucified victim.
Grayling argues that Christian stories repeat ancient mythic patterns, that European intellectual categories came from Greece and Rome, and that Christian ethics later imported Stoic cosmopolitanism.
Christian metaphysics and later European Christian thought depended extensively on imported Platonist and Greek philosophical ideas.
The move broadens the classical-source case beyond ethics by arguing that core Christian doctrines and major Christian thinkers relied on Greek philosophy.
Holland's presentation of Christianity as a distinctive and foundational source of Western moral and intellectual assumptions.
Grayling contends that changing beliefs about death required Christianity to adopt Platonist doctrines and that Augustine, Aquinas, and later European thought remained grounded in Greek philosophy.
Although Christianity absorbed Jewish, Persian, Greek, and Roman influences, it radically reconfigured them through the crucified God and universal divine kinship.
This directly rebuts reduction to classical borrowing while explaining the distinctive Christian transformation that allegedly produced universal dignity and solidarity.
Grayling's claim that Christianity was a familiar mythic covering whose ethics and metaphysics were imported from classical philosophy.
Holland concedes multiple cultural influences but argues that Paul transformed them by proclaiming a crucified slave as God's son and extending divine love and childship to marginalized people.
Claims of Christianity's uniqueness overlook common ancient divine-son motifs, while Christian suppression of pagan culture was real despite ultimately failing.
The move contests both Christian novelty and the benign transmission narrative, supporting the opposing genealogy through continuity and cultural suppression.
Holland's claim that the crucified Son of God radically overturned Greco-Roman assumptions and elevated socially insignificant people.

Grayling treats divine sonship as commonplace, argues that early Christians tried to efface pagan culture, cites institutional suppression, and notes that Christianity later had to absorb classical philosophy.
There is no evidence of a systematic Christian campaign to erase classical literature, and Christian copyists preserved central works of ancient culture.
The move answers a major historical objection to Christian inheritance by presenting Christians as transmitters rather than systematic destroyers of classical culture.
Grayling's allegation that early Christians destroyed pagan books, institutions, and the surviving record of classical civilization.

Holland cites Christian copying of Homer and other classical authors, challenges Grayling's account of Byzantine indifference, and characterizes the destruction narrative as an Enlightenment-era myth.
Substantial Christian preservation of classical texts began only centuries after suppression, while Arab and Persian scholars preserved and transmitted much of the corpus.
This qualifies the Christian-preservation defense and restores non-Christian transmission and the early medieval decline as important parts of the classical legacy's survival.
Holland's assertion that Christians continuously preserved classical culture and that the contrary account is historically false.

Grayling says monastic copying accelerated roughly three centuries after Theodosius, credits Muslim scribes and translators, and points to limited publication and knowledge between the fourth and eighth centuries.
Monastic preservation of classical texts was systematic, whereas the story of wholesale Christian erasure arose from later Protestant and Enlightenment mythmaking.
The move reinforces the Christian-transmission case and challenges the historical framing underlying the opposing account of Christianity's relation to antiquity.
Grayling's claim that meaningful Christian copying was delayed and that the early Christian centuries transmitted comparatively little classical learning.

Holland lists classical authors copied in Latin and Byzantine settings, denies a systematic campaign of elimination, and attributes the contrary picture to anti-monastic Protestant narratives later recast by the Enlightenment.

The principal wellsprings of Western ethical reflection, equality, cosmopolitan obligation, natural liberty, and friendship arose in Axial Age and classical philosophy rather than uniquely in Christianity.
This supplies the con side's principal historical genealogy for Western values and directly contests the claim that Christianity uniquely introduced dignity, equality, or ethical concern.
The earlier claim that Christianity uniquely elevated ordinary and enslaved people into persons possessing dignity and intrinsic worth.
After the moderator restates the dispute about Christianity's treatment of the lowly, Grayling locates ethical inquiry in the Axial Age, Socrates, Aristotle, and especially Stoic cosmopolitanism.
Paul's declaration that social distinctions are overcome through Christ constitutes a radical break from classical societies that regarded foreigners as naturally fitted for enslavement.
The move directly contrasts Pauline universalism with Greek and Roman assumptions about natural slavery, supporting the pro side's account of Christianity's distinctive moral revolution.
Grayling's contention that Christian ethical tropes were appropriated from an already established classical philosophical foundation.

Responding to Grayling's classical genealogy, Holland contrasts Aristotle's natural-slavery doctrine and ancient ethnic hierarchy with Paul's erasure of Jew-Greek, slave-free, and male-female distinctions.
Pauline Christianity gave every person bodily integrity, constrained male sexual power, reshaped marriage, and underlies modern expectations represented by the Me Too movement.
This offers a concrete causal case for Christianity transforming inherited moral assumptions and argues that even avowedly secular modern sexual ethics remain saturated with Christian teaching.
Grayling's broader position that modern ethical values derive primarily from classical sources rather than a distinctive Christian moral transformation.

Holland contrasts Roman masters' accepted sexual use of slaves with Pauline bodily sanctity and self-restraint, then treats contemporary demands for male restraint as evidence of Christianity's lasting influence.
Paul's teachings were not consistently egalitarian, and Christianity's long tolerance of misogyny and racial slavery undermines claims that it powerfully transformed ancient moral practice.
The move attacks the proposed Christian causal mechanism using counterexamples from scripture and Christian history, arguing that alleged pagan defects persisted throughout Christian civilization.
Holland's argument that Pauline sexual morality established bodily dignity and that modern Me Too ethics reveal Christianity's saturating influence.
Grayling agrees with modern equality and restraint but disputes Holland's Pauline genealogy, citing restrictions on women and the survival of racial slavery deep into Christian history.
The abolition of racial slavery was driven chiefly by Quaker and evangelical convictions that Christian universalism and divine law required equal treatment across racial boundaries.
Abolition is a major test case for the motion, and this move attributes its decisive moral impetus to radical Protestant interpretations embedded in the broader Christian inheritance.
Grayling's claim that Christianity's failure to end slavery for fifteen centuries demonstrates its weakness as a source of humane values.

Holland explains the racialization of Atlantic slavery and argues that Pauline equality, inward divine law, Quaker activism, and evangelical mobilization transformed abolition from a minority view into policy.
Enlightenment rights and international abolitionism were not a clean secular break but fused Protestant, Catholic, and Enlightenment ideas derived from a shared Christian conceptual matrix.
The move states the pro side's overarching thesis that apparently secular Enlightenment reforms remain transformations of Christian concepts rather than independent alternatives to Christianity.
Grayling's explanation that weakening denominational control enabled people to think differently and ultimately made the overthrow of slavery possible.

Holland insists abolition was evangelical, explains how Catholic rights language and Enlightenment equality joined it, and identifies their common ancestry as the fundamental disagreement with Grayling.
The Renaissance and scientific revolution liberated the European mind by recovering classical learning, rejecting inherited authority, and grounding inquiry in observation and reason.

This provides the con side's alternative explanation for Western intellectual modernity, locating decisive progress in emancipation from ecclesiastical authority and recovery of classical human capacities.
Holland's claim that the Enlightenment and even anti-Christian secularism remain iterations of concepts generated within Christian civilization.

Grayling acknowledges medieval church power but argues that classical recovery, human dignity, empirical correction of authorities, and independent reason gradually freed European thought from dogmatic control.

Repeated Christian renaissances, universities, scientific lawfulness, reformations, and even the Enlightenment express recurring Christian narratives of rational order and liberation from superstition.

The move directly reframes the con side's strongest intellectual-history examples as products of Christian institutions and recurring Christian narratives, reinforcing the pro side's general causal thesis.
Grayling's account of one Renaissance and scientific revolution liberating European reason from the church's long-standing hegemony and dogmatic authority.

Holland argues there were multiple Christian renaissances, links universities and scientific law to belief in a rational creator, and treats reform and Enlightenment as recurring Christian renewal patterns.

Secular humanism and Europe's ethical vocabulary arise chiefly from classical philosophy, Enlightenment reason, shared humanity, and sympathetic reflection rather than a particular Judeo-Christian root.
This is Grayling's concluding statement of the con case, directly identifying the sources of ethical obligation, humanism, scientific method, and rational moral consideration outside Christianity.
Holland's contention that secular humanists remain essentially Christian because their dignity, equality, and universal-love ideals are steeped in Judeo-Christian ethics.

Grayling traces ethical concepts to the Socratic, Aristotelian, and Stoic traditions, defines humanism through reasoned sympathy for diverse experience, and roots its modern form in Enlightenment rationalism.
Christian stories achieved a uniquely saturating cultural power, and modern human dignity and rights ultimately descend from the Genesis doctrine that humanity bears God's image.

This is Holland's concluding explanation of how Christianity shaped Western moral intuitions beyond philosophy, grounding contemporary human uniqueness, dignity, and rights in pervasive biblical narrative.
Grayling's concluding claim that secular humanism, rational ethics, and concern grounded in common humanity owe more to classical antiquity and Enlightenment thought.

Holland accepts mediated Greek influence but emphasizes Christianity's emotionally powerful stories, centuries of cultural saturation, inherited theological assumptions, and the imago Dei as the source of Western dignity.
The geographic concentration of organized humanism in historically Christian societies supports treating humanism as a culturally contingent Protestant inheritance.
This supplies an empirical cultural-distribution argument for the central claim that modern secular humanism remains historically dependent on Christianity.
Grayling's position that secular humanism derives chiefly from rational Enlightenment and classical sources.
After tracing human dignity to Genesis, Holland points to where humanist gatherings occur and characterizes modern humanism as culturally Christian despite its rejection of God.
Humanistic ethics arose independently in Greek, Chinese, Jain, and Buddhist traditions through reflection on shared humanity rather than Christian revelation.
Independent pre-Christian and non-Christian examples directly challenge the motion-level claim that Western humanistic concern owes its substance to Christianity.
Holland's claim that humanism is culturally contingent on Christianity and resembles a godless form of Protestantism.
Grayling invokes several civilizations and a story of spontaneous mutual concern to argue that compassion and human connection need neither Christian mythology nor Christian transmission.
General compassion may recur across cultures, but the distinctive idea that every human possesses rights and exceptional dignity originates in Christian myth.
The distinction between widespread compassion and specifically Christian universal dignity is Holland's central answer to evidence of ethical parallels elsewhere.
Grayling's examples of pre-Christian and non-Christian compassion as evidence that humanism develops independently.
Holland concedes the broader phenomenon of concern while arguing that Grayling selectively adopts parallels to universalize values actually inherited from Christian European culture.
Christianity cannot claim ownership of humanistic impulses that have clear analogues predating it across multiple civilizations, and it offers no unique major innovation.
The demand for a uniquely Christian contribution tests the historical originality required for Christianity to receive primary credit for modern human values.
Holland's accusation that secular humanists appropriate scattered foreign parallels to disguise their values' Christian derivation.
Grayling reverses the appropriation charge and asks Holland to identify any ethical or metaphysical Christian novelty without an earlier source, parallel, or analogy.
Christian civilization introduced distinctive categories and institutions, including lifelong matrimony, modern sexual classifications, secularism, modern science, and exceptional human dignity.
The enumerated innovations directly answer the challenge to identify uniquely Christian contributions and reconnect those contributions to universal Western values.
Grayling's challenge to name one significant Christian innovation lacking a precedent or analogue in another civilization.
Holland names several allegedly novel Christian inheritances, emphasizes dignity grounded in divine image, and argues that Western universalism itself perpetuates Christianity's universal mission.
Holland's proposed Christian novelties are either not uniquely Christian, not major achievements, or already represented in much older religious materials.
This attacks the uniqueness and significance of Holland's principal examples, which were offered as the direct proof of distinctive Christian contribution.
Holland's list of lifelong monogamy, sexual categories, secularism, science, and human dignity as Christian innovations.
Grayling invokes Stoic universalism, questions monogamy as an achievement, and argues that distinctions involving same-sex conduct already appear in ancient scriptural law.
Ancient prohibitions on same-sex acts are not equivalent to the modern category of homosexuality, whose conceptual structure remains a distinctively Christian inheritance.
The conceptual distinction defends one concrete example in Holland's list and illustrates his broader thesis about unnoticed Christian assumptions in secular thought.
Grayling's claim that the heterosexual-homosexual distinction was already drawn in ancient Pentateuchal prohibitions.
Holland argues that Grayling mistakenly maps a modern identity category onto an ancient description of conduct, thereby displaying the very Christian conceptual inheritance he denies.
The few distinctive Christian contributions Holland identifies are ethically dubious or are remedies for divisions that Christian institutions themselves helped create.
The response contests both the value and explanatory force of Holland's examples, especially the claim that secularism should count as a positive Christian innovation.
Holland's defense of modern sexual categories and secularism as historically distinctive products of Christian civilization.
Grayling separates historical distinctiveness from valuable contribution, then treats secularism as an institutional response to a church-created struggle with temporal authority.
Even secularism and other assumptions shared by contemporary atheists descend through medieval theology to Gospel materials and ancient scriptural fragments.
This final historical synthesis reinforces Holland's overarching causal claim that apparently secular modern categories remain products of Christian theological development.
Grayling's portrayal of secularism as merely a church response to an institutional problem of its own making.
Holland traces the relevant distinction backward through theological development and the Gospels, generalizing that many modern assumptions derive from long-past theology and scripture.
The Christian-origin thesis reflects Holland's desire for that conclusion more than a neutral inference from the historical evidence.
Although brief, this challenges the evidential method underlying Holland's repeated genealogical claims and crystallizes Grayling's final objection to the thesis.
Holland's sweeping conclusion that nearly all shared modern assumptions can be traced to theologians and Christian scripture.
Grayling closes by alleging motivated interpretation, while the exchange ends on the shared methodological principle that historical evidence should determine the conclusion.
